newsitem.title: MEXICO: Polish airplane firm plans to open Mexican factory.
newsitem.headline: Polish airplane firm plans to open Mexican factory.

text.p: Polish airplane-maker Panstwowe Zaklady Lotnicze (PZL) plans to open a new factory in Mexico in 1998 as part of the company's strategy of boosting sales in the Americas, the company's president and chief economic officer said.
"I think that in 1998 we'll have the first planes coming off the line in Mexico," Ryszard Leja told Reuters at Aeroexpo '97, an international aviation trade show and convention.

PZL -- a Warsaw-based joint venture of the Polish government, which owns 51 percent, and a consortium of Polish companies owning 49 percent -- has annual sales of $50 million, selling primarily its trainers and crop dusters in Europe, Africa, the Mideast and Latin America.
It already has a factory making planes in Indonesia, Leja said.
PZL's Wilga 80 and Koliber 150 models, both of which carry U.S. Federal Aviation Regulation 23 safety approvals, are among the biggest sellers.
The Koliber, a four-seater often used for training, "is capable of competing with any similar aircraft in America," a PZL brochure claims.
Leja said PZL sold two Wilgas and one Koliber during the convention, a good start on the company's goal of selling 10 planes a year in Mexico until the factory comes on line.
Leja said he did not want to disclose the site of the factory.
PZL is one of Poland's most successful export companies since the end of communist rule. The company was founded in 1928, predating communism by nearly two decades.
"Now, let's say, we are free and we can go everywhere, so we decided to come to Latin America," Leja said.

PZL currently imports propellers and engines from the United States for assembly in Poland. The company can cut costs and reduce production time by importing the U.S.-made parts to Mexico for assembly there, he said.
PZL's best sales pitch is cost. "We don't know the prices of our competitors but we know we are cheaper," Leja said.
PZL, whose Latin American customers are mostly military and agricultural, plans a bigger push once the Mexican plant comes on line.
"The idea is to start up the first assembly line in Meixco and from there create our own designs with the help of Polish technology," said Jorge Aiza, PZL's Mexican representative.
